name: Alter-globalization
summary: Alter-globalization is the global-justice movement of the World Social Forum and Attac, which accepts international cooperation but opposes corporate-led, neoliberal globalization. Its demands are fair rather than free trade, cancelling poor countries' debt, taxing financial transactions and abolishing tax havens, protecting public services and food sovereignty, demilitarisation, and democratic control of the UN, IMF, World Bank and WTO. It favours participatory democracy and non-violent resistance, and its programmes include gender equality and ecological limits.
scope: The mainstream of the movement as stated in its own texts: the WSF Charter of Principles (2001), the Attac platform (1998), the 2005 Porto Alegre Manifesto (signed personally by nineteen figures), the 2006 Bamako Appeal and the Assembly of Social Movements declarations (Caracas 2006, Nairobi 2007, Istanbul 2008, Belem 2009). It excludes nationalist or protectionist critics of globalization and treats insurrectionary currents as a fringe. The Charter forbids the Forum itself from taking positions, so positions are read from the movement's programmes and assemblies, not the Forum as a body.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Bamako Appeal treats health care as a non-market service whose public provision must be reinstated and expanded, and the Manifesto and Caracas call back universal access and oppose privatising health.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says the market may have a place but not the predominant one, rejects the claim that private capitalist firms are the most efficient, and puts resources under political rather than market decision.

public-ownership.rationale: The Caracas call declares water, land and energy sources public goods belonging to the people and condemns privatisation; the Bamako Appeal puts resources and key social services outside the market.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says redistribution of wealth through taxation should be defended and extended, and the Attac platform calls for taxing capital revenue and speculative transactions.

unions-good.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls the right to form unions one of workers' two main weapons and urges a worldwide united labour front built on unions opening to other movements.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Bamako Appeal treats natural resources and basic services as common wealth outside the market, and Belem backs ownership forms that serve the social interest, so private property is not held fundamental.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The Bamako Appeal demands enforceable public standards for corporate responsibility in international law and investment codes setting the rights of nations and workers; the Charter opposes corporate-led globalization.

cut-welfare.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for reinstating and expanding social services and the Manifesto demands social protection and pensions for all; the 2008 assembly appeal rejects dismantling welfare.

worker-ownership.rationale: The Belem declaration lists cooperative, communal and collective property among ownership forms favouring the social interest, and the Bamako Appeal backs mutualisation and workers' authority in firms, without ruling out other forms.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The Bamako Appeal names democracy in the enterprise a major demand, recognising the authority of workers, users and collectives and rejecting the shareholders' dictatorship.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The Manifesto says all inhabitants of the planet must have the right to social protection and pensions, and the Bamako Appeal makes migrant workers' rights and residence-based voting a basic concern.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says democracy must give a strategic position to the poor and oppressed, and the Manifesto aims its taxes and aid at the needs of the poorest.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The Charter and Attac platform locate poverty and exclusion in capitalist and financial globalization, not in population growth.

production-for-use.rationale: The Charter says the Forum values centring economic activity on meeting people's needs and respecting nature, and the Bamako Appeal opposes the logic of capitalist profit.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The Belem declaration says the system rests on exploiting labour and transferring resources from workers to the capitalist class, and the Attac platform says capital income grows at the expense of labour income.

collective-farming.rationale: The Bamako Appeal and Belem declaration build food sovereignty on peasant and small family farms with access to land, not on collective farming.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The Belem declaration says the capitalist system results in bloody wars and the Bamako Appeal ties wars over oil and water to the commodification of life, though neither says great-power war is inevitable.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says an alternative socialist society must be fully democratic, blames the Soviet system's failures on denial of freedom, and says no social policy justifies suppressing freedom.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says solidarity cannot rest on ignoring the conflicts of interest between classes and nations.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: The Bamako Appeal speaks of a united front of workers North and South who all suffer from neoliberal globalization and says its anti-imperialism does not set Southern peoples against Northern ones.

no-bailouts.rationale: The 2008 European assembly appeal condemns rescue plans using public money to refund private banks' deficits while social needs go unmet, though Belem prefers nationalising banks.

taxation-theft.rationale: The Manifesto and Bamako Appeal call for new international taxes and for extending redistribution through taxation, the opposite of treating taxation as theft.

bound-labor.rationale: The Bamako Appeal makes access to land a basic right for peasants and aims to abolish exploitation by class, which is incompatible with labour bound to a lord.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says access to land for all peasants is a basic right needing land-system reforms and sometimes agrarian reform, and opposes land monopolisation by elites and firms.

positive-liberty.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says political democracy is incomplete and cannot last without social rights and while inequality persists, and asserts economic and social rights as the base of democracy.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The Belem declaration backs forms of ownership that favour the social interest and the Bamako Appeal manages resources as common wealth for humanity's needs.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: The Manifesto calls for mechanisms of progressive upward equalisation of social and environmental norms, as set by ILO conventions, in trade in goods and services.

free-trade.rationale: The Manifesto rejects free-trade agreements and WTO rules, the Bamako Appeal calls free trade the enemy of real integration, and the Attac platform attacks the MAI and the Transatlantic Market.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Cancelling Southern countries' external debt is the first point of the Manifesto and a founding Attac aim, and a top mobilisation priority in the Bamako Appeal.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The Manifesto says rich countries' public development aid should imperatively reach 0.7 per cent of GNP, and the Attac platform sends Tobin-tax revenue to poor countries' health, education and food security.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The Manifesto and Bamako Appeal call for democratising the UN, bringing the IMF, World Bank and WTO under it, strengthening the General Assembly and creating a world parliament of peoples, while also guarding national sovereignty.

nation-first.rationale: The Charter seeks a globalization of solidarity and democratic international institutions, and the Bamako Appeal builds an internationalism of Northern and Southern peoples.

open-borders.rationale: The Nairobi assembly backed a day of action for migrants' rights and the free movement of peoples, but the Bamako Appeal also calls the nation the strategic level of democracy and treats borders as a basis of popular sovereignty.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The Nairobi assembly backed migrants' rights and the free movement of peoples, though the Bamako Appeal also treats borders as a basis of popular sovereignty.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for citizenship acquired through residence, with voting rights following.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The Bamako Appeal affirms the autonomy of nations and peoples, calls capitalism's expropriation of the South colonial-type theft, and builds an anti-imperialist internationalism.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Belem declaration demands peoples' sovereignty and autonomy with the right to self-determination, and the Charter backs national sovereignty within democratic international institutions.

civilizational-union.rationale: The Bamako Appeal tells African integration to abandon designs founded on race or culture, and warns against confining identities in para-ethnic or para-religious ghettos.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The Bamako Appeal tells African integration to abandon designs founded on race or culture and seeks a universal civilization rather than integration by ancestry.

dominated-front.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for a Bandung of the peoples of the South and a peoples' front of the South able to check the imperialism of the dominant economic powers and US military hegemony.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Bamako Appeal builds an anti-imperialist internationalism and calls for dismantling foreign bases and ending occupations, the opposite of expansion abroad.

national-mission.rationale: The Bamako Appeal rejects the dominant conception of democracy advanced by the United States and Western powers and the imposition of any single universal recipe.

war-builds-character.rationale: The Charter commits the Forum to peaceful, solidarity-based relations among peoples and opposes violence as a means of social control.

military-superiority.rationale: The Bamako Appeal and Manifesto call for dismantling foreign military bases and troop deployments, and the Bamako Appeal for abolishing nuclear arsenals.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for prohibiting the manufacture and use of nuclear weapons and destroying all existing arsenals.

collective-defense.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for a campaign to dissolve NATO and rejects NATO interventions outside Europe.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for dissolving NATO and dismantling all military bases abroad, and the Manifesto for removing foreign troops except under a UN mandate.

force-without-un.rationale: The Manifesto allows foreign troops only under an explicit UN mandate, and the Bamako Appeal and Caracas assembly reject preventive war.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The Manifesto asks full recognition of indigenous peoples' political, cultural and economic rights, including access to natural resources, and Belem calls for rights to land and territory.

workers-nation.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for reorganising a worldwide working class and transnational union structures, while also organising nationally.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Charter bars parties from the Forum and upholds real, participatory democracy against totalitarian views, and the Bamako Appeal gives pre-eminence to building democracy after the Soviet failures.

democracy-best.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for democracy without pre-assigned limits and says no social policy justifies denying freedom or basic rights.

workers-councils.rationale: The Bamako Appeal wants democracy in firms and from below but says participation completes and deepens representative democracy rather than replacing it.

strong-leader.rationale: The Charter upholds participatory democracy and the Bamako Appeal says active citizens should manage all aspects of life and calls for renewed attention to authority and hierarchy.

state-harmful.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls national democracy the strategic level, defends public policy against neoliberalism and public services, and seeks state sovereignty over institutions like the IMF.

decide-locally.rationale: Pleyers distinguishes a local current that places change in local self-government from a state current that places it in national policy, and the Bamako Appeal both reinforces the local level and calls the nation strategic.

natural-rulers.rationale: The Charter condemns all forms of domination and the subjection of one person by another, and the Bamako Appeal wants active citizens to manage every area of social life.

total-state.rationale: The Charter opposes all totalitarian and reductionist views of economy, development and history and the use of violence as State social control.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Manifesto and Bamako Appeal demand autonomy for journalists, an end to media concentration and support for non-profit and alternative media.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for women's equal representation in institutions (parity) and stronger legal provisions for gender equality.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says no social policy can justify the absence of freedom and disrespect of basic rights and condemns US torture and violations of liberty.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The Bamako Appeal blames the failure of the Soviet system and decolonisation regimes largely on their denial of freedom and says no social policy can justify its absence.

state-as-business.rationale: The Bamako Appeal rejects reducing citizens to consumers and wants economy and finance placed in service of a societal programme rather than markets.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The Bamako Appeal asserts collective rights and peoples' right to struggle against oppression beside civil, political and social rights, and the Manifesto recognises indigenous peoples' rights.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Charter commits the Forum to respect universal human rights and all citizens, men and women, of all nations, and condemns all domination of one person by another.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The Manifesto calls for public policies against all discrimination, sexism, xenophobia, antisemitism and racism.

women-must-cover.rationale: The Bamako Appeal affirms women's right to control their bodies and life choices and denounces patriarchal norms resting on religious and cultural standards.

traditional-family.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says the family remains the main place where girls and women are domesticated and calls for eradicating patriarchy in its forms.

abortion-legal.rationale: The Bamako Appeal lists the right of abortion with contraception and the choice to have a child among women's basic rights over their bodies.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The Bamako Appeal defines patriarchy as male domination reinforced by the state, family codes and institutions, and ties it to imperialism and neoliberalism.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Bamako Appeal affirms absolute equality of the sexes in law and in fact and calls for legal provisions for effective equality.

restore-past-order.rationale: The Bamako Appeal wants a universal civilization that looks to the future without nostalgia.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The Manifesto calls for public policies against all racism and discrimination, and the Bamako Appeal condemns segregation and discrimination on ethnic bases.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The Manifesto and Charter oppose racism and xenophobia in all forms, and the Bamako Appeal condemns ethnic segregation and discrimination.

population-transfer.rationale: The Manifesto calls for public policies against xenophobia and racism, and the Bamako Appeal defends migrants' rights and residence-based citizenship.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The Bamako Appeal condemns the individualist, consumerist culture of capitalism and sets solidarity above competition.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says solidarity has historically served production better than competition and seeks to diminish the role of competition among workers, nations and peoples.

minority-language-support.rationale: The Bamako Appeal affirms the right to express oneself in one's own language and urges teaching and promoting national languages and funding translation into low-income languages.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Caracas assembly called for mobilisation in defence of free, public and secular education.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The Bamako Appeal makes the politically active citizen responsible for managing all aspects of social life, and the Charter makes citizen participation central.

political-violence-never.rationale: Researchers find most global justice protesters non-violent while small groups used more disruptive forms, and the Charter backs non-violent resistance while opposing only state violence.

direct-action.rationale: Assemblies praise electoral victories of allied governments and urge keeping autonomy from them, and Pleyers finds currents split between local action, advocacy and the state route.

means-match-ends.rationale: The movement practises horizontal participatory and deliberative decision-making internally and as its aim, and the Bamako Appeal stresses its democratic practice as a renewal of political culture.

experts-over-public.rationale: Researchers find the movement rejects vertical structures and demands deeper citizen inclusion in decisions, and the Bamako Appeal puts citizens in charge.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The Charter bars military organizations from the Forum and commits it to non-violent social resistance.

vanguard-party.rationale: The Charter makes the Forum a non-party space and the Bamako Appeal asks unions to cooperate with movements without subordinating them to any party.

expand-nuclear.rationale: The Belem climate justice declaration lists more nuclear power among false neoliberal solutions to climate change.

limit-growth.rationale: Belem rejects the development model of never-ending growth and consumption, but the Bamako Appeal wants poor countries to be able to industrialise while rich ones cut emissions.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: The Manifesto demands urgent steps against climate change, the Bamako Appeal demands rich countries cut carbon dioxide output and abolish pollution rights, and Belem calls for climate justice now.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The Belem declaration calls for a society respecting nature's rights and living in harmony with the world, and the Charter commits to respecting nature.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The Manifesto calls for ending excessive use of non-renewable energy, and Belem rejects the fossil-based growth model.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says concentrated media carry neoliberal ideology and format minds to make the existing order look inevitable and desirable.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: The Belem declaration describes a system built on transferring resources from the periphery to the centre, and the Manifesto says Southern debt has been paid many times over and keeps humanity's majority under creditor control.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says there is no single universal recipe in the political or economic spheres and affirms the autonomy of peoples and nations, while also rejecting the Western definition of democracy.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: The Attac platform calls for stopping the spread of pension funds, and the Bamako Appeal defends retirement based on solidarity between generations.

single-official-language.rationale: The Bamako Appeal affirms the right to express oneself in one's own language, opposes an English monopoly and calls for supporting national and low-income languages.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The Bamako Appeal condemns capitalism's individualist and consumerist culture and the wasteful consumer it produces.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for an anti-imperialist order that checks dominant powers, rejects control by the United States and defends the autonomy of peoples.

corporate-influence.rationale: The Charter says governments and international institutions serve large multinationals, and the Attac platform says policy expresses the interests of corporations and financial markets.

job-guarantee.rationale: The Manifesto says everyone must have the right to employment, an imperative of public policy at national and international level.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The Manifesto and Bamako Appeal call for the right of all citizens to access information and to inform.

local-production.rationale: The Bamako Appeal puts the satisfaction of local needs ahead of world-market arrangements and promotes local circuits between production and consumption.

informal-organisation.rationale: Researchers find horizontal networks without formal leaders, yet the Bamako Appeal calls for unions and a worldwide labour front.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The Bamako Appeal wants national law to decide the local economic system and respect for sovereignty against the IMF and WTO, while also backing UN reform, international courts and a world parliament.

religious-nation.rationale: The Bamako Appeal warns against para-religious identity ghettos and seeks a universal civilization, and the Charter is non-confessional.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The Bamako Appeal rejects hegemony by the United States and advocates a multipolar order of equal peoples.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The Bamako Appeal opposes privatising water even through public-private partnerships, and the Caracas assembly condemned privatising communications, health and education.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Belem declaration says the radical alternative that ends capitalism must also end patriarchal domination and will necessarily be feminist, and the Bamako Appeal ties patriarchy to neoliberalism.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The Nairobi assembly backed international mobilisations for sexual diversity and equality and criticised groups hostile to sexual rights.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Bamako Appeal asserts the rights to freedom of organization and expression as the base of democratic freedoms.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls the North's patenting of the South's genetic resources colonial-type theft and builds an anti-imperialist internationalism.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The Charter upholds participatory democracy, the Bamako Appeal demands participation in workplaces and neighbourhoods, and researchers find participatory and deliberative democracy central to the movement.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The Bamako Appeal aims to abolish exploitation by class, gender, race and caste, ties patriarchy to imperialism and neoliberalism, and says gender must be considered in every recommendation.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for dissolving NATO and urges a Bandung of the peoples of the South against the dominant powers.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: The Bamako Appeal asks respect for state sovereignty against IMF, World Bank and WTO actions and a return to national law over unnegotiated international decisions, and the Caracas assembly called protests against their policies.

property-franchise.rationale: The Bamako Appeal makes democracy open to all, with residence-based citizenship and voting rights.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Manifesto opposes racism by public policy and the Bamako Appeal gives residents voting rights and condemns ethnic segregation.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says media concentration serves neoliberal interests and calls for laws curbing it and shielding journalists from owners.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says political democracy cannot last while inequality persists and attacks the shareholders' dictatorship, and the Attac platform says finance bypasses democratic institutions.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The Bamako Appeal and Manifesto demand public social services and social protection guaranteed to all.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Bamako Appeal condemns the family model in which men hold authority over its members and demands equality of the sexes in law and fact.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says local democracy should make citizenship possible through residence, with voting rights following.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for prohibiting nuclear weapons, destroying arsenals and dismantling military bases abroad.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: The Manifesto, Bamako Appeal and Belem declaration all demand dismantling foreign military bases, and the Nairobi assembly backed a conference to abolish them.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The Attac platform complains that capital revenue grows at the expense of labour revenue and proposes taxing capital revenue.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The 2008 European assembly appeal calls for developing public services in water, health, housing, electricity and transport, and the Caracas call declares water a public good.

gm-crops.rationale: The Manifesto says countries must be able to ban production and import of genetically modified organisms, and the Bamako Appeal links GMOs to dependency and environmental destruction.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: The Bamako Appeal and Caracas assembly reject preventive war, and the Manifesto allows foreign troops only under a UN mandate.

free-public-college.rationale: The Caracas assembly called for mobilisation to defend free, public education, including university strikes.

pollution-taxes.rationale: The Manifesto calls for international taxes on activities with large greenhouse-gas emissions, though the Bamako Appeal also relies on binding cuts.

future-generations.rationale: The Bamako Appeal bases resource use on the right to a decent life for present and future generations, and the Charter commits to respecting nature for future generations.

arms-reduction.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for abolishing nuclear arsenals and dismantling foreign bases, and the Manifesto proposes taxing the arms trade.

capital-controls.rationale: The Bamako Appeal lists controlling the flow of capital, especially speculative capital, as part of reorganising the monetary system, and the Manifesto proposes taxing capital flows.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The Bamako Appeal wants transnational union structures able to negotiate with transnational employers.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for economic reorganisation of the global system, including new WTO rules, regulation of investment and a reformed monetary system, and the Manifesto calls for deep reform of international institutions.

nature-as-capital.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says resources must not be treated as commodities, and the Belem declaration rejects carbon trading as a neoliberal illusion and speaks of nature's rights.

farm-price-support.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for guaranteed minimum domestic farm prices, price-control coordination and gradually raising farm prices to protect peasants.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: The Bamako Appeal calls for prohibiting nuclear weapons and destroying all existing arsenals.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Bamako Appeal points to women's unequal access to material, financial and natural resources and calls for effective legal equality.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says democracy is empty without social progress and rejects the dominant market-tied conception of elections-based democracy.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: The Manifesto demands the right of all citizens to access information and to inform.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Bamako Appeal demands absolute equality of the sexes in law and fact and women's equal representation in institutions.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says patriarchy spread with monotheistic religions and is supported by cultural standards and religious values that appropriate women's capacities.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The Bamako Appeal condemns torture and violations of liberty by US agents and insists on basic rights and freedoms.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says land, water and the planet's resources are common wealth managed for humanity's needs, with the North owing ecological debts to the South.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The Manifesto says all inhabitants must have the right to social protection and pensions, and the Bamako Appeal calls for universal public services.

no-business-privileges.rationale: The Attac platform attacks agreements that give investors all the rights, and the Bamako Appeal asks codes of investment that set the rights of nations and workers.

national-resource-control.rationale: The Bamako Appeal says resource decisions rest on the political powers of nations and peoples, used according to each country's needs, and condemns the North's patenting of the South's genetic resources.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: A tax on speculative currency transactions is Attac's founding demand and the second point of the Manifesto.

multipolar-world.rationale: The Bamako Appeal's first programme is a multipolar world system founded on peace, law and negotiation, rejecting US control of the planet.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The movement's own texts (the Charter, Porto Alegre Manifesto, Attac platform, Bamako Appeal and Assembly declarations) state no position that settles this.
